summary: Introduces two technology-independent extensions to GMPLS. One defines a Data Channel Switching Capable switching type for interfaces that switch a whole digital channel. The other defines a new label type that lets a set of channels be described together.

eli5.summary: Some network switches move one whole channel at a time, like swapping an entire train car. This adds a new way to label those switches and to name a group of channels together.

questions: what is the generalized channel_set label
what is data channel switching capable
what is switching type 125 in gmpls
subtitle: A new GMPLS switching type for whole-channel ports and a label that names a whole set of channels at once.

tldr.problem: GMPLS had no switching type for interfaces that switch everything arriving on a port, and no compact way to signal many data plane labels, such as up to 4096 VLAN IDs, for one LSP.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 6002 defines the Data Channel Switching Capable (DCSC) switching type, value 125, and a Generalized Channel_Set label whose subobjects carry runs of subchannels, based on the LABEL_SET object of RFC 3473.
tldr.outcome: Both extensions are technology independent. They arose from Ethernet services work but can be used with any switching technology controlled by GMPLS.

today: RFC 6002 is a Proposed Standard published in October 2010. The metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It updates RFC 3471, RFC 3473, RFC 3945, RFC 4202, RFC 4203 and RFC 5307.

sections.title: Two Generic GMPLS Extensions
sections.content:
RFC 6002 describes two technology-independent extensions to Generalized MPLS (GMPLS). Both were first defined for Ethernet services (see RFC 6004 and RFC 6005), but are generic and may help any switching technology controlled by GMPLS.

The first is a new switching type, Data Channel Switching Capable (DCSC), for interfaces that switch the whole digital channel presented on a single-channel interface. The second is a new generalized label, the Generalized Channel_Set Label, which lets more than one data plane label be controlled as part of one Label Switched Path (LSP).
sections.eli5: There are two new ideas. One names a kind of switch that moves a whole plug at a time. The other lets you write one label that covers many channels.

sections.title: Data Channel Switching Capable
sections.content:
Existing GMPLS switching types cover packet (PSC), frame (L2SC), time-slot (TDM), frequency (LSC) and fiber (FSC) granularity. Missing was switching where all data received on an ingress port is switched through the network to an egress port. It resembles the opaque single wavelength case in RFC 4202, but is not limited to optical technology. FSC is similar but limited to fiber ports and supports several channels per fiber.

DCSC fills the gap. The RFC notes that 'port switching' would be a more intuitive name but collides with PSC. Interfaces that inherently carry multiple channels, such as WDM and channelized TDM, are excluded. Anything that can be seen as one digital channel is included, for example concatenated TDM, line-encoded interfaces, or Ethernet terminated at the port level where all traffic on a port goes to a physical port at the LSP egress.

DCSC uses the value 125. It travels in the Interface Switching Capability Descriptor used by OSPF (RFC 4203) and IS-IS (RFC 5307), which are not otherwise changed. It may be used with the Generalized Label Request object of RFC 3473 or the Generalized Channel_Set LABEL_REQUEST object below, and port labels SHOULD be used for DCSC LSPs.
sections.eli5: Imagine a switchboard that moves a whole plug instead of single wires inside it. DCSC is the name for that kind of switch.

sections.title: The Channel_Set Label Objects
sections.content:
The motivation was carrying one or more VLAN IDs. Simply concatenating labels, as RFC 4606 does, was judged impractical given up to 4096 VLAN IDs. The LABEL_SET object of RFC 3473 is the foundation, but the Channel_Set label puts the full set in one object instead of many.

The Generalized Channel_Set LABEL_REQUEST object has the same format as the Generalized LABEL_REQUEST object and uses C-Type 5. It signals that the Channel_Set LABEL object is to be used. The Generalized Channel_Set LABEL object (Class 16, C-Type 4) carries one or more labels that can all be used equivalently in the data path of one LSP. It MUST be used on LSPs that use the Channel_Set LABEL_REQUEST, and it is processed per RFC 3473. Make-before-break procedures SHOULD be used when modifying it.

The other label objects and subobjects from RFC 3473 (SUGGESTED_LABEL, LABEL_SET, ACCEPTABLE_LABEL_SET, UPSTREAM_LABEL, RECOVERY_LABEL and the Label ERO and RRO subobjects) can carry the new label type without redefinition, because they are label-type agnostic.
sections.eli5: Instead of mailing a hundred separate tickets, you send one envelope with a list of all the seats you can use.

sections.title: The Channel_Set Subobject
sections.content:
The label object holds Channel_Set subobjects. Each subobject is a multiple of 4 bytes, at least 4, and has these fields: Action (8 bits), Number of Subchannels (10 bits), Label Type (14 bits), the subchannels, and any padding.

Range actions SHOULD be used when possible to keep the object small. Since 10 bits limit the count to 1024, more subchannels need several subobjects, which may make a Path message larger than one unfragmented IP packet.

A count of zero is special in a LABEL or UPSTREAM_LABEL object. It means the subchannels in that direction MUST match those in the reverse direction's label object. No subchannels are included and only one subobject may be present. Zero MUST NOT be used in both objects of the same LSP; a Resv with zero in both gets a ResvErr.

Padding is needed only if the subchannels leave the subobject not 32-bit aligned. It MUST make the subobject aligned, MUST be zero on transmission and ignored on receipt, and SHOULD be passed through unmodified by transit nodes. The Label Type field uniquely identifies the size of each subchannel.
sections.eli5: Each list in the envelope says what to do, how many items it has, and what kind they are. Blank space at the end just fills it out to a neat size.

sections.title: Handling Unsupported Nodes
sections.content: A transit or egress node that does not support DCSC treats it like any unsupported switching type. Per RFC 3473 it MUST send a PathErr with 'Routing problem/Unsupported Encoding'. A node that does not support the Channel_Set formats answers the Channel_Set LABEL_REQUEST with a PathErr 'Unknown object C_Type', per RFC 3209. In both cases the ingress node then notifies the requesting application user as appropriate.
sections.eli5: If a node does not know the new words, it politely sends back an error note, and the sender tells whoever asked.

sections.title: IANA Assignments
sections.content: IANA assigned value 125, Data Channel Switching Capable (DCSC), in the Switching Types section of the GMPLS Signaling Parameters registry. In the RSVP PARAMETERS registry it assigned C-Type 5 (Generalized Channel_Set) under the LABEL_REQUEST class number 19, and C-Type 4 (Generalized Channel_Set) under the RSVP_LABEL class number 16.
sections.eli5: The official list keeper wrote the new numbers in its book.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC adds new object formats to GMPLS signaling but no new messages and no change to the relationship between adjacent LSRs. It therefore adds no security considerations. The text points to RFC 3473 for the relevant ones and to RFC 5920 for the MPLS and GMPLS security framework.
sections.eli5: Nothing new here is risky by itself, so the old safety rules still apply.
